theory.overview: Memory allocators are the unsung heroes of software performance. Every object creation, array allocation, and string concatenation goes through an allocator. Understanding allocation strategies—from simple bump allocators to sophisticated slab and pool allocators—helps you write memory-efficient code, diagnose performance bottlenecks, and make informed decisions about custom allocators for performance-critical systems. This chapter explores how memory managers work under the hood.

sections.title: The Memory Hierarchy
sections.content: Memory exists in a hierarchy of speed and size: CPU registers (fastest, bytes), L1/L2/L3 caches (fast, KB-MB), RAM (medium, GB), SSD/HDD (slow, TB). Allocators work with virtual memory provided by the OS, mapping pages (typically 4KB) as needed. The allocator's job is to satisfy allocation requests quickly while minimizing fragmentation and maximizing cache locality. Poor allocation patterns cause cache misses, page faults, and performance degradation.

sections.title: Bump Allocation (Arena)
sections.content: The simplest and fastest allocator: maintain a pointer to the next free byte. To allocate N bytes, check if space remains, return current pointer, bump pointer by N. O(1) time, extremely cache-friendly (sequential allocation). Used in garbage collectors for young generation, and in arena allocators where all objects have the same lifetime. Limitation: cannot free individual objects—entire arena must be freed together.

sections.title: Free List Allocators
sections.content: To support individual deallocation, free list allocators maintain a linked list of free memory blocks. When allocating: search list for block of sufficient size, remove from list, return to user. When freeing: add block back to list, optionally coalesce adjacent free blocks. Variants include first-fit (first large enough), best-fit (smallest adequate), and segregated fits (separate lists by size class). malloc/free in C typically use these techniques.

strategies.name: First Fit
strategies.pros: Fast, tends to use low addresses

strategies.name: Next Fit
strategies.description: First fit, starting from last position

sections.title: Slab and Pool Allocators
sections.content: When allocating many objects of the same size (common in kernels, games, databases), slab allocators excel. A slab is a contiguous memory region divided into fixed-size slots. Allocation: pop from free list of appropriate slab. Free: push back to list. No searching, no fragmentation for same-size objects, excellent cache locality (objects of same size often accessed together). Linux kernel, Redis, and many games use slab allocators.
benefits: Zero internal fragmentation for fixed sizes

sections.title: Buddy System
sections.content: The buddy system divides memory into power-of-2 sized blocks. Requests are rounded up to next power of 2. When a block of size 2^k is needed but unavailable, a larger 2^(k+1) block is split into two 'buddy' blocks of size 2^k. One is used, one is freed. On deallocation, buddies are coalesced back if both free. Used in Linux kernel for page allocation. Efficient for variable sizes while limiting fragmentation.
process: Use one buddy, free the other
On free: check if buddy free, coalesce to 8KB

sections.title: Modern Allocator Design
sections.content: Production allocators like jemalloc, tcmalloc, and mimalloc combine multiple strategies. Thread-local caches avoid contention—each thread has small per-thread arenas. Size classes segregate common allocation sizes (8, 16, 24... bytes) for O(1) lookup. Large allocations go directly to the OS. Deferred coalescing and lazy freeing improve performance. These allocators achieve near-zero overhead for typical application patterns.

features.name: Thread Caching
features.description: Per-thread arenas avoid locks and false sharing

keyConcepts.name: Internal Fragmentation
keyConcepts.description: Wasted space inside allocated blocks. Request 100 bytes, allocator gives 128 (power-of-2). 28 bytes wasted.
keyConcepts.mitigation: Size classes, exact-fit for common sizes

keyConcepts.name: External Fragmentation
keyConcepts.description: Free memory scattered in small blocks, unable to satisfy large requests despite total free space being sufficient.

keyConcepts.name: False Sharing
keyConcepts.description: Different threads accessing different variables that happen to be on the same cache line, causing cache invalidation thrashing.

keyConcepts.name: Cache Locality
keyConcepts.description: Temporal (reused soon) and spatial (nearby access) locality. Allocators can optimize for both.
keyConcepts.allocatorRole: Sequential bump allocation has excellent spatial locality

complexity.freeListAllocate: $O(F)$ where $F$ = free list length, $O(1)$ for segregated
complexity.buddyAllocate: $O(\log n)$ where $n$ = memory size, often $O(1)$ in practice

steps.title: Receive Allocation Request
steps.description: Application requests N bytes. Allocator determines strategy based on size and context.

steps.title: Select Size Class
steps.description: Round up to next size class (e.g., 64→64). Find appropriate slab or free list for that size.

steps.title: Allocate from Slab
steps.description: Pop from free list (O(1)), or allocate from bump pointer within slab. Return pointer to caller.

steps.title: Track Allocation Metadata
steps.description: Store size and slab info (for freeing). Some allocators use header, some use parallel data structures.

steps.title: Handle Free Request
steps.description: On free, determine slab from pointer, push to free list. Check for coalescing if using buddy system.

steps.title: Background Maintenance
steps.description: Periodically return empty slabs to OS, coalesce buddies, or trigger GC if integrated with garbage collector.

practiceProblems.title: Bump Allocator Limitation
practiceProblems.description: Why can't bump allocators free individual objects?
practiceProblems.answer: No tracking of object boundaries or which objects are free vs allocated
practiceProblems.explanation: Bump allocators only track the high-water mark (bump pointer). They don't know where individual objects are or which are freed.

practiceProblems.title: Internal Fragmentation
practiceProblems.description: Allocator gives power-of-2 blocks. Request 100 bytes, get 128. What's internal fragmentation?
practiceProblems.explanation: Internal fragmentation is the unused space inside an allocated block. 28 of 128 bytes are wasted for this allocation.

practiceProblems.title: Slab Allocator Speed
practiceProblems.description: Why are slab allocators O(1) for both allocation and free?
practiceProblems.answer: No search needed—push/pop from size-specific free list
practiceProblems.explanation: Slabs maintain a free list per size class. Allocation pops head, freeing pushes to head. Both are simple pointer operations.

practiceProblems.title: Buddy System Split
practiceProblems.description: Buddy system has 16KB block available. Request 5KB. What happens?
practiceProblems.answer: 16KB split to 8KB+8KB, one 8KB split to 4KB+4KB. Return one 4KB, free other 4KB and 8KB.
practiceProblems.explanation: Round 5KB up to 8KB? No, to power of 2 is 8KB. Wait, actually usually 5KB→8KB. Let me re-read. Actually typically buddy uses power of 2. Request 5KB→8KB. 16 split to two 8s. One used, one free.

practiceProblems.title: False Sharing
practiceProblems.description: What is false sharing and why does it hurt performance?
practiceProblems.answer: Different threads modify different variables on same cache line, causing cache invalidation
practiceProblems.explanation: Cache lines are 64 bytes. Even if threads touch different variables, if they're on same line, each write invalidates the other's cache copy, forcing reload from memory.
hints: Cache line is unit of coherence
Same line = shared even if different variables

practiceProblems.title: Segregated Fit Advantage
practiceProblems.description: Why is segregated fit faster than general free list?
practiceProblems.answer: O(1) lookup for common sizes—no search through mixed-size blocks
practiceProblems.explanation: General free list may need to scan many blocks to find fit. Segregated has separate lists by size, so first block is always adequate.

practiceProblems.title: Thread Cache Benefit
practiceProblems.description: Why do modern allocators use per-thread caches?
practiceProblems.answer: Avoid locks and false sharing between threads
practiceProblems.explanation: Without thread caches, all threads contend on global lock. With thread caches, most allocations are lock-free from thread-local storage.

practiceProblems.title: Coalescing Necessity
practiceProblems.description: Why is coalescing (merging adjacent free blocks) important?
practiceProblems.answer: Prevents external fragmentation, enables larger allocations
practiceProblems.explanation: Without coalescing, adjacent small free blocks stay separate. A request for their combined size would fail despite total free space being sufficient.

practiceProblems.title: Arena Allocation Use Case
practiceProblems.description: When is arena (bump) allocation the best choice?
practiceProblems.answer: Many objects with same lifetime, like in a compiler's AST for one function
practiceProblems.explanation: Arena shines when all objects die together. Fast allocation, no per-object free, free entire arena at once when done.

practiceProblems.title: Memory Alignment
practiceProblems.description: Why do allocators often align allocations to 8 or 16 byte boundaries?
practiceProblems.answer: Hardware requires aligned access for performance, some types require specific alignment
practiceProblems.explanation: Unaligned memory access is slower (multiple cache/DRAM accesses) or crashes on some architectures. Also enables SIMD instructions that require alignment.

minigame.title: Memory Master
minigame.description: Manage a virtual heap efficiently! Allocate, free, and organize memory to minimize fragmentation and maximize speed. Compare different allocation strategies and become a memory management expert.
instructions: Receive allocation requests of various sizes
Place blocks in the heap visualization

levels.name: Free List Fighter
levels.description: Handle allocations and frees with fragmentation

visualizer.title: Memory Allocator Visualizer
visualizer.description: Watch how different allocation strategies manage memory in real-time. Visualize heap layout, fragmentation, and allocation patterns. Compare bump, free list, slab, and buddy allocators side by side.

snippets.title: Bump Allocator
snippets.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

@dataclass
class BumpAllocator:
    '''Simple bump pointer allocator.
    Fast O(1) allocation, no individual free().
    Reset frees everything at once.'''
    size: int
    
    def __post_init__(self):
        self.memory = bytearray(self.size)
        self.bump_ptr = 0
        self.allocations = 0
    
    def allocate(self, n: int) -> Optional[int]:
        '''Allocate n bytes, return pointer or None'''
        if self.bump_ptr + n > self.size:
            return None  # Out of memory
        
        ptr = self.bump_ptr
        self.bump_ptr += n
        self.allocations += 1
        return ptr
    
    def reset(self):
        '''Free all memory at once'''
        self.bump_ptr = 0
        self.allocations = 0
    
    def used(self) -> int:
        return self.bump_ptr
    
    def available(self) -> int:
        return self.size - self.bump_ptr

# Demo
arena = BumpAllocator(size=1000)

# Allocate various objects
ptr1 = arena.allocate(100)  # Object 1: 100 bytes
ptr2 = arena.allocate(50)   # Object 2: 50 bytes
ptr3 = arena.allocate(200)  # Object 3: 200 bytes

print(f'Allocated at: {ptr1}, {ptr2}, {ptr3}')
print(f'Used: {arena.used()} bytes, Available: {arena.available()} bytes')

# Can't free individual objects
# But can reset entire arena
arena.reset()
print(f'After reset: Used {arena.used()}, Available {arena.available()}')

# New allocations start from beginning
ptr4 = arena.allocate(300)
print(f'New allocation at: {ptr4} (should be 0 after reset)')

# Real-world use case: temporary compiler allocations
class CompilerArena:
    '''Use arena for AST nodes during parsing one function'''
    def __init__(self):
        self.arena = BumpAllocator(size=10000)
    
    def new_node(self, size: int = 32):
        ptr = self.arena.allocate(size)
        if ptr is None:
            raise MemoryError('Arena exhausted')
        return ptr
    
    def finish_function(self):
        # All AST nodes for this function die together
        self.arena.reset()
        print('All function AST nodes freed at once!')

compiler = CompilerArena()
# Parse function, allocate many nodes
for i in range(10):
    compiler.new_node(40)
print(f'Nodes allocated, arena used: {compiler.arena.used()}')
compiler.finish_function()
